source: Alaboudi, LaToza (2020) Using hypotheses as a debugging aid
finding: Controlled experiment on whether hypotheses drive debugging success. Developers hold few hypotheses and most are wrong early.
numbers: 20 developers in the control condition (60 sessions in all), 3 tasks. Two hypotheses per defect on average. Stage 1: 3 of 27 hypotheses correct (11%). Stage 2: 9 of 35 (25%). Stage 3: 15 of 38 (39%).
limits: Web-API tasks (DOM, React, CSS animation); small N; 2.6 h sessions.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis quality, not hypothesis use, is the bottleneck. Predict-then-observe only helps if the prediction comes from a plausible hypothesis.

source: Alaboudi, LaToza (2020) Using hypotheses as a debugging aid
finding: A correct hypothesis early predicts later success.
numbers: Logistic regression over 60 sessions: a correct hypothesis at stage two gave 5 times higher odds of fixing the defect (p = 0.01).
limits: Correlational; some people with correct hypotheses still failed (needed docs, mapping to code).
agent_relevance: Gate: before spending budget on experiments, check that a candidate hypothesis is specific and testable.

source: Alaboudi, LaToza (2020) Using hypotheses as a debugging aid
finding: Offering fault locations did not help. Offering candidate hypotheses did.
numbers: Ordinal logistic regression: potential hypotheses odds ratio 6.24 (p = 0.03); fault locations OR 1.4 (p = 0.64); years of experience OR 1.14 (p = 0.04). Correct hypotheses with fault locations: 45% (stage 2), 60% (stage 3) vs control 45% and 75%. Task 3 success: 6/6 with hypotheses vs 5/6 fault locations.
limits: Hypotheses were hand-picked from Stack Overflow, one correct and one incorrect per task; cells of 6-8; no significant time difference (p about 0.61).
agent_relevance: Giving rival hypotheses, each with a way to test it, beats telling the agent where to look. Supports an operator that generates several rival hypotheses with tests.

source: Alaboudi, LaToza (2020) Using hypotheses as a debugging aid
finding: Participants said aids helped only when they were partly on track.
numbers: Survey quote: fault locations 'helpful only when I was slightly confused'. 25 recruited, 5 used as pilots.
limits: Self-report.
agent_relevance: Hints help when the solver is near the answer; may do little when lost. A boundary condition for any rescue operator.

source: Alaboudi, LaToza (2021) An exploratory study of debugging episodes
finding: Naturalistic study of how real debugging time is split.
numbers: 15 live-streamed sessions, 11 professional developers, 30 hours; 2137 debugging activities and 1407 programming activities coded. Debugging came once every 8 minutes. Debugging was 13-95% of session time (mean 48%).
limits: Self-selected live-streamers, open-source work, thinking aloud.
agent_relevance: Real debugging is mostly edit and browse, not tidy hypothesis testing. A scaffold forcing explicit hypotheses imposes more structure than people show.

source: Alaboudi, LaToza (2021) An exploratory study of debugging episodes
finding: Inspecting program state (the observe step) is rare and slow.
numbers: Inspecting state: twice per episode on average, 8% of episode time, 53 s each time (longest of any activity). Tools: log statements 70%, breakpoints 30%. Run and observe output: 84% manual, 16% automated tests. After inspecting, developers edited 65% of the time.
limits: Per-episode means with wide spread (SD 105 s).
agent_relevance: Experiments cost real time for people. For an agent, observation is cheap code execution, so it can afford more predict-then-observe loops.

source: Alaboudi, LaToza (2021) An exploratory study of debugging episodes
finding: Long episodes behave differently from short ones.
numbers: 80% of episodes were short. 23 long vs 23 short compared. Short episodes: editing and testing took 88% of time. Long episodes: browsing rose from 1.3% to 18%, many more kinds of activity, later first edit. Consulting outside resources occurred in only 21% of episodes.
limits: Exploratory, not causal.
agent_relevance: Most debugging cost sits in the long tail. Put hypothesis discipline on stuck cases, not easy ones (fits G1).

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: AutoSD makes an LLM run Zeller-style cycles: hypothesis, prediction, experiment with a real debugger, conclusion, then patch. Repair rate stays close to plain LLM.
numbers: Defects4J v1.2: 76 correct patches (AutoSD) vs 87 (LLM-Base, ChatGPT), 10 patches each. Defects4J v2.0: 113 vs 110. Max 3 iterations. Recoder got 24 and 11; finetuned InCoder 41 and 28 (Jiang et al.).
limits: Method-level fault location given; ChatGPT; one template.
agent_relevance: The scientific-debugging format does not raise repair rate by itself; it makes reasoning inspectable. Do not expect an accuracy gain from the format alone.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Real debugger execution is what makes the loop useful. When the LLM imagines the debugger output, results get worse.
numbers: With simulated debugger output, individual runs giving a plausible patch fell from 73% to 63%. A DONE conclusion with real execution was 12.4 points more likely to be plausible; with simulated output it was 11 points less likely.
limits: ARHE benchmark of mutation-made Python bugs; easier than real bugs.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2/G3: the observe step must come from code, not from the model's guess.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: The model's own 'I have enough information' signal is mildly informative.
numbers: For bugs with a plausible patch and a DONE prediction, 89% were correctly fixed; plausible patch without DONE, 82%. Defects4J: 100 sampled patches with and without DONE labelled by hand.
limits: Small gap; manual labels on a sample.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis-confirmed stop signal carries modest information (89% vs 82%): a hint, not proof.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Repair gain depends on model strength.
numbers: Across CodeGen-6B, Codex and ChatGPT on ARHE, AutoSD rose toward LLM-Base as models improved. CodeGen-6B zero-shot failed (returned the original code); few-shot it fixed 44 bugs.
limits: Three model families only.
agent_relevance: The hypothesis-experiment loop needs a capable base model.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Human study on whether the scientific-debugging explanation helps judge a patch.
numbers: 20 participants (14 students, 6 professionals), 12 bugs (6 ARHE, 6 BugsInPy); explanation shown for a random 3 of 6 per participant. Judgement time similar, no statistically significant difference in any case. Accuracy higher with explanation in 7 of 12 bugs, including 5 of 6 real bugs. 70% wanted explanations with repair tools; 55% satisfied with the scientific-debugging detail.
limits: Small N; accuracy not tested for significance; two bugs got worse.
agent_relevance: Explanations raise review accuracy modestly at no time cost, at least for real bugs.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Explanations can mislead.
numbers: On ARHE105, participants who answered wrongly accepted AutoSD reasoning without scrutiny. On BIP003 the explanation made respondents more cautious. For the two incorrect real patches (BIP002, BIP004) accuracy improved with explanations.
limits: One of 12 sampled problems.
agent_relevance: A fluent hypothesis trace can persuade a reader of a wrong fix. A checker should not rely on the story (G5).

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a human: LDB
finding: LDB shows the model real intermediate variable values after each basic block and asks it to judge each block against the task, like breakpoints.
numbers: Gains up to 9.8 points over baseline across HumanEval, MBPP and TransCoder with GPT-3.5, CodeLlama-34B and StarCoder-15B. Self-Debugging variants (explain, trace) changed StarCoder HumanEval by -0.6 to +0.6 (baseline 39.0).
limits: Compared with a reproduced Self-Debugging; weak models gain little.
agent_relevance: Real intermediate state checked block by block beats model-written dry-run traces. Evidence for observed state over imagined state.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a human: LDB
finding: LDB still helps strong seed programs.
numbers: HumanEval, seeds from Reflexion (91.5%): LDB with GPT-3.5 95.1 (+3.6), GPT-4 96.9 (+5.4), GPT-4o 98.2 (+6.6).
limits: HumanEval near ceiling; small test sets.
agent_relevance: Verification against runtime state adds value on top of a strong generator.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a human: LDB
finding: Self-debugging stalls early; LDB keeps improving across turns.
numbers: Figure 3: Self-Debugging nearly stops improving after about 2-3 iterations; LDB keeps rising slowly.
limits: Taken from text and figure caption, not a raw table.
agent_relevance: Cap iterations that bring no new real evidence at about 2-3 (matches G1).

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are modest once compute is counted; the feedback step is the bottleneck.
numbers: Drawing 2 samples then 10 repairs each (up to 22 samples) gave 0.97x the pass rate of plain pass@22; another setting gave 1.05x over pass@20. On APPS GPT-4 beat baseline by up to 8%; GPT-3.5 gained up to 34% on competition-level only.
limits: APPS 300 tasks (180 interview, 60 competition, 60 intro); GPT-3.5 near ceiling on HumanEval.
agent_relevance: Compare any debug loop against simply sampling more at equal compute. Repair gains are not free.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Better diagnosis is what matters; humans diagnose far better than the model.
numbers: 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 16 participants, 2 human feedbacks per program, 25 repairs sampled each. Repair success with GPT-4's own feedback 33.30% overall vs 52.60% with human feedback (1.58x). Intro 42.64 vs 62.21, interview 19.33 vs 45.67, competition 3.67 vs 14.67.
limits: Small human study; about 1 hour each; feedback time not tracked.
agent_relevance: Improve the step that turns observations into a correct causal explanation, not retrying. Strongest numeric case for hypothesis quality in LLMs.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: A stronger feedback model lifts a weaker repair model at every budget.
numbers: Replacing Code Llama's feedback with GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback, and GPT-3.5's with GPT-4's, beat both i.i.d. baseline and self-repair at all budgets.
limits: Costs a stronger model.
agent_relevance: Cross-model diagnosis helps; same-model diagnosis likely shares blind spots (G4).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking the model to review its own answer does not help and often hurts.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0.
limits: Math and question answering, not debugging.
agent_relevance: Rereading a hypothesis without new evidence is useless. Direct support for G2.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Earlier reported gains came from an oracle that told the model when it was wrong.
numbers: With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5, CSQA 75.8 to 82.0, HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and more often turned correct into wrong than wrong into correct.
limits: Oracle uses ground truth, so these are upper bounds.
agent_relevance: Explains why debug loops with real test results work and loops without them do not. A predict-then-observe check supplies the oracle-like signal.

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2023) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Few-shot rubber-duck self-debugging: the model explains its code and reads execution results.
numbers: Spider text-to-SQL: +2-3% with code explanation, +9% on the hardest queries. TransCoder and MBPP: up to +12% with unit-test feedback. Matches or beats baselines sampling over 10x more candidates.
limits: Biggest gains need unit tests; strong Codex/GPT models.
agent_relevance: Explain-then-check works when a test result exists; read with Huang to see that the signal, not the explanation, does the work.

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2023) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Execution feedback helps more than explanation alone; trace adds a small extra.
numbers: Execution trace feedback improved over simple feedback by up to about 1% on other benchmarks. Explanation alone improved TransCoder by 2-3%.
limits: LDB paper reports trace-based self-debugging can fail on weaker models.
agent_relevance: The first real failure message does most of the work; detailed traces add little.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench
finding: Benchmark of 4,253 bugs across syntax, reference, logic and multiple-error classes (C++, Java, Python), built from LeetCode with implanted bugs.
numbers: Findings: LLM debugging falls short of human performance; multiple and logic errors much harder than syntax and reference; runtime feedback helps syntax and reference bugs but is unhelpful for logic errors.
limits: Implanted bugs, zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Logic bugs are where hypothesis-driven reasoning is needed and raw error output does not carry the answer.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent
finding: Interface design for the agent changes outcomes as much as the model.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: SWE-agent GPT-4 Turbo 18.0% vs shell-only 11.0% vs RAG 2.67%. Full SWE-bench 12.47% (286/2294). Edit with linting 18.0 vs without 15.0 vs no edit tool 10.3. Search: summarised 18.0, none 15.7, iterative 12.0. Runs begin with reproduction or localisation.
limits: Ablations on 300 instances; single run, wide per-instance variance.
agent_relevance: Immediate checking of every edit (lint) and a reproduce-first habit help; a predict-then-observe step fits the reproduce-first pattern.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval
finding: Predicting what code outputs (the predict half of predict-then-observe) is hard even for top models.
numbers: 800 Python functions. GPT-4 without CoT: 67% input prediction, 63% output prediction. GPT-4 with CoT: 74.8% input, 81.9% output. Best open models 47% and 44%. HumanEval gains did not transfer.
limits: Short 3-13 line functions.
agent_relevance: Model predictions of execution are wrong 1 time in 5 even with CoT, so a mismatch may mean a bad prediction rather than a bad hypothesis.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval
finding: CoT helps output prediction more than input prediction, and only for stronger models.
numbers: CoT helps Code Llama 34B and GPT-4 on both tasks, GPT-3.5 only on output, Code Llama 13B on neither. CoT widens the pass@5 minus pass@1 gap.
limits: Depends on model size.
agent_relevance: Forward simulation gains from stepwise writing; backward inference (what input causes the failure) does not. Diagnosis is the weakest step.

source: Yang, Prabhakar, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) InterCode
finding: Interactive execution loops sharply beat single-turn generation for strong models, barely for weak ones.
numbers: InterCode-SQL success single turn to Try Again (n=10): GPT-4 9.1 to 73.7; GPT-3.5 10.5 to 47.3; text-davinci-003 7.4 to 15.6; Vicuna-13B 2.6 to 6.3; StarChat-16B 8.9 to 9.7.
limits: SQL environment; Try Again stops on reward 1, which leaks the verdict.
agent_relevance: Observing real results is huge for strong models and near zero for weak ones: a capability threshold.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal self-reflection after failing tests lifts coding scores, but only when the tests are good.
numbers: HumanEval Python 0.80 to 0.91; MBPP Python 0.80 to 0.77 (worse); HumanEval Rust 0.60 to 0.68; MBPP Rust 0.71 to 0.75. False-positive rate (tests pass, solution wrong): 0.01 HumanEval Python vs 0.16 MBPP Python.
limits: Same model writes tests and code.
agent_relevance: A failed gain on MBPP Python: self-written tests that pass wrongly end the loop too early. Direct case for G3.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Removing the written diagnosis removes the gain.
numbers: Rust ablation: without the natural-language reflection after failed tests, performance did not improve over baseline. On HotPotQA, reflection added about 8% absolute over episodic memory alone.
limits: One model family.
agent_relevance: Writing a diagnosis (a hypothesis) before retrying matters; blind retry is no better than baseline on hard tasks.
